status_terms.key_figure: any transmitter at whose level the isnād branches to several transmitters (p. 143)
status_terms.CL: the earliest key figure who can be proven to have circulated a given tradition (p. 143)
status_terms.PCL: any key figure above the CL who can be proven to have transmitted a variant of the CL tradition (pp. 143-144)
status_terms.SCL: seeming CL: an apparent oldest key figure that turns out not to be the real CL (p. 144)
status_terms.(S)PCL / (S)CL: Pavlovitch's hedged label for a key figure whose status is plausible but not proven (e.g. p. 172)
status_terms.CR: Collector: compiler of an extant ḥadīth collection, chronicle or biographical lexicon (p. 146)

tradition.description: The tradition opening Khudhū ʿan-nī ... qad jaʿala l-lāhu la-hunna sabīlan with the dual-penalty maxim (virgin: flogging and banishment; non-virgin: flogging and stoning). Pavlovitch calls it 'the ʿUbāda tradition' while stating that it cannot be ascertained as going back to ʿUbāda; he also uses 'dual-penalty maxim', 'penal maxim' and 'prophetic dictum'.

structure_of_study.part: Literary analysis of the stoning concept in exegesis (Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, Abū ʿUbayd, al-Muḥāsibī, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Marwazī)
Isnād-cum-matn analysis: non-revelation cluster (Shuʿba, Hushaym, additional clusters, summary)
Isnād-cum-matn analysis: revelation cluster (Ibn Abī ʿArūba, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan sub-clusters)
Approaches to reconstruction, earliest collections, organic development, summary table
General conclusions (literary vs isnād-cum-matn; isnād analysis vs isnād-cum-matn; Qurʾān-sunna discontinuity)

grouping_criterion.text: The bundle is split by one salient matn feature: presence or absence of a preamble describing the symptoms of revelation descending on the Prophet. The non-revelation group is analysed first, then the revelation group.

explicitly_excluded.text: The Māʿiz b. Mālik tradition, the employer's wife (ajīr) tradition, the Sharāḥa tradition, the stoning-verse reports and other pro- or anti-dual-penalty traditions appear only in the literary analysis; Pavlovitch says a full isnād-cum-matn study of them would exceed a journal article and confines himself to the ʿUbāda tradition. The two Ibn ʿAbbās traditions in Abū ʿUbayd are discussed only as exegetical context.

common_link.summary: Pavlovitch rejects a single first-century CL. For the non-revelation (dual-penalty) tradition the earliest historically tenable CL is Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj; Hushaym b. Bashīr, Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān and Wakīʿ are later CLs of derivative variants. The revelation preamble goes back to a short exegetical tradition of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī on Q 4:15, whose CL is Jarīr b. Ḥāzim. The compound revelation tradition has no established CL; its ascriptions to Ibn Abī ʿArūba, Qatāda and al-Ḥasan are treated as back-projections.

reasoning.point: Matns of the Shuʿba cluster are homogeneous; variations are clause rearrangements that do not affect meaning and fit spontaneous oral transmission, pointing to a common source and independent transmission.
Isnād support: Shabāba b. Sawwār is a PCL, Ghundar a cautious (S)PCL; with at least two key figures transmitting from Shuʿba, the remaining Ibn al-Jaʿd isnāds gain credibility.

Hushaym's parallel version adds qualifiers (one hundred lashes, one year) that elucidate the vaguer unqualified wording, so the unqualified Shuʿba form is earlier and the tradition existed by the second quarter of the second century AH.
Hushaym and al-Qaṭṭān based their versions on Shuʿba's tradition (drawn in Diagram 4 as 'source of Hushaym' and 'source of al-Qaṭṭān').
In the worst-case scenario Shuʿba is the oldest historically tenable CL of the non-revelation tradition; his relationship with Qatāda is hard to prove.
Shuʿba is the earliest disseminator of the non-revelation tradition (conclusions).

caveats.point: Shuʿba's version is reconstructed from later collections; clauses 3-4 may be an expansion, and the exclamation Khudhū ʿan-nī plus the Q 4:15 reference may not have been part of the original matn.
Ibn al-Jaʿd, the main knot above Shuʿba, is quoted only in single strands without a CR and would have to be a near-centenarian.

pavlovitch_identifications.tradition: Hushaym's variant of the non-revelation tradition

reasoning.point: Two unambiguous PCLs (Yaḥyā b. Yaḥyā al-Tamīmī, Qutayba b. Saʿīd) plus two direct CRs (Ibn Ḥanbal, Saʿīd b. Manṣūr).
Four consistent matns (Abū Dāwūd, al-Maḥāmilī, al-Shāshī, al-Nasāʾī) sharing ramyun/rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra; no line proves an earlier CL (Ibn Abī ʿArūba).
Ibn Ḥanbal and al-Ṭaḥāwī cite identical matns; nothing supports a CL older than Wakīʿ.

pavlovitch_identifications.tradition: al-Ḥasan's exegetical tradition (core of the revelation preamble)
pavlovitch_identifications.common_link: Jarīr b. Ḥāzim (d. 170/786-7) as CL; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as the most likely originator

reasoning.point: Al-Ṭayālisī and ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, via Jarīr, both preserve a preamble citing Q 4:15; stripping intrusions yields a common core attributable to Jarīr.

Yazīd b. Hārūn's isnād via Maymūn also reaches al-Ḥasan, an important but not unambiguous indication of al-Ḥasan's role; ʿAbd al-Razzāq's Khudhū! Khudhū! and a line ending at al-Ḥasan support the same reading.
Al-Ḥasan most likely circulated a short tradition: Q 4:15 was revealed and the Prophet said 'Take them! Accept them!' (i.e. these verses).

Abū ʿUbayd (a direct CR) and al-Shāshī no. 1325 differ insignificantly, making Yazīd a fully-fledged CL; his variant is later than the reconstructed Muʿādh and Qatāda versions and cannot be traced to al-Ḥasan.
Revelation isnāds show a welter of attributions to Ibn Abī ʿArūba, Qatāda and al-Ḥasan carried by single strands and intermittent CR quotations; uncertainty is high even for Ibn Abī ʿArūba.

Traditionists who held the maxim to be revealed attached the preamble to the earlier non-revelation dictum and attributed the compounds to the lower links of the non-revelation isnād; random back-projection explains the untidy isnāds and mixed matns.
Qatāda and Ibn Abī ʿArūba cannot be shown to be CLs of the compound; the analysis of their contribution met insoluble contradictions.

argument.point: Before analysis: Qatāda fits chronologically between Mujāhid and Muqātil and could have circulated the maxim as a prophetic tradition; hypothesis needs isnād-cum-matn testing.

Shuʿba and al-Qaṭṭān (via Ibn Abī ʿArūba) converge on Qatāda, and Hushaym's line reaches al-Ḥasan, an optimistic scenario pushing the tradition into the late first century AH; tempered because al-Qaṭṭān's link via Ibn Abī ʿArūba and Hushaym's via Manṣūr b. Zādhān are unproven, and neither Hushaym's nor al-Qaṭṭān's matn derives from al-Ḥasan or Qatāda.
Tentatively conceding Ibn Abī ʿArūba and Shuʿba as PCLs of Qatāda, Qatāda would have related the penal maxim alone.

Scenario: Qatāda altered al-Ḥasan's exegetical tradition, kept the revelation clause (anna l-nabiyya unzila ʿalay-hi), dropped the Q 4:15 citation and attached the maxim; Shuʿba, Hushaym and al-Qaṭṭān then dropped the awkward preamble. Alternative: Qatāda transmitted al-Ḥasan's tradition intact, which would make Shuʿba's ascription to Qatāda a concealment.
Neither Qatāda nor Ibn Abī ʿArūba can be excluded as the first to alter al-Ḥasan's tradition; collection evidence places the merger long after their deaths.

other_candidates_discussed.status: CL status not proven; reconsidered with hesitation

argument.point: Non-revelation: only al-Qaṭṭān and one al-Ṭabarī strand (a copy of Shuʿba) reach him; no CL earlier than al-Qaṭṭān.
Revelation: one hypothetical (S)PCL (Yazīd b. Zurayʿ) and two doubtful key figures; isnād evidence insufficient, though the matns show three consistent traits.
Since Shuʿba and al-Qaṭṭān lack the preamble, Ibn Abī ʿArūba probably knew the maxim without it; scenario of him altering al-Ḥasan's tradition is examined and found problematic.

other_candidates_discussed.candidate: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (as source of the dual-penalty maxim)

argument.point: Al-Ḥasan most likely held that offenders be treated according to Q 4:15; a dual-penalty raʾy would contradict that, so the maxim was ascribed to him by someone who wanted the sunna, not scripture, to regulate zinā.
The maxim was not a factor in legal debate in al-Ḥasan's floruit.

other_candidates_discussed.status: rejected as CL instead of Hushaym

argument.point: No evidence allows treating him as CL in place of Hushaym.

competing_claims.claim: The most likely CL of the ʿUbāda bundle is Qatāda b. Diʿāma; the basic elements of the legal maxim are most probably due to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and discussion of the punishment may go back to the Prophet's lifetime; Juynboll concedes that the strands converging in al-Ḥasan are technically deficient and look like back-projections, yet still counts al-Ḥasan among the earliest jurists to stress these punishments.

pavlovitch_response.point: Juynboll's conclusion is at odds with his own isnād-analytical criteria and most likely derives from Schacht's principle that short legal maxims reflect an early stage of jurisprudence.
If al-Ḥasan formulated the maxim, it is odd that his contemporary Mujāhid did not know it.

Juynboll's method dwells on isnāds and leaves the wording of the 'basic elements' to intuition. Isnād-cum-matn analysis accepts his supposition only in linking al-Ḥasan to the question of the zinā penalty; al-Ḥasan in fact endorsed treating offenders by Q 4:15, and the dual-penalty maxim was not a factor in his time, still less in early Islam.

partial_common_links.name: ʿAlī b. al-Jaʿd
partial_common_links.status: CL or PCL on matn grounds; isnād evidence equivocal
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭaḥāwī and Ibn Ḥibbān match his matn exactly (Abū ʿAwāna's collective version excepted), but all lines from him are single strands forming a spider with no CR; dying 70 lunar years after Shuʿba he would be a near-centenarian (Ibn Saʿd: ~24 at Shuʿba's death; came to Basra 156/773-4); Ibn al-Madīnī reportedly abandoned him because his wording from Shuʿba varied. After Ghundar and Shabāba are weighed, his isnāds 'enjoy greater chance' of being authentic.

partial_common_links.name: Muḥammad b. Jaʿfar Ghundar
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn Ḥanbal (direct CR) and al-Ṭabarī (via Ibn al-Muthannā) have identical matns differing from Ibn al-Jaʿd in a way suggesting an independent source; Muslim's and al-Bazzār's versions via Ibn al-Muthannā are confused, so only one CR plus one single strand remain.

partial_common_links.name: Shabāba b. Sawwār
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn Abī Shayba (direct CR) and al-Shāshī (via ʿĪsā b. Aḥmad) give essentially Ibn al-Jaʿd's matn with negligible differences.

partial_common_links.name: Abū al-Naḍr Hāshim b. al-Qāsim al-Laythī
partial_common_links.evidence: Abū ʿUbayd (direct CR) agrees with Ibn al-Jaʿd, but the second line is Abū ʿAwāna's confused collective isnād, leaving a single attribution.

partial_common_links.name: Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā
partial_common_links.evidence: Al-Ṭabarī, Muslim and al-Bazzār quote him with three different matns; the discrepancy lowers Ghundar to (S)PCL.

partial_common_links.name: Qutayba b. Saʿīd
partial_common_links.evidence: Al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī (direct CRs), Ibn Ḥibbān (via Ibn al-Junayd) and Abū ʿAwāna (collective) are sufficiently homogeneous.

partial_common_links.name: Yaḥyā b. Yaḥyā al-Tamīmī
partial_common_links.evidence: Muslim and al-Marwazī (direct CRs) identical; al-Bayhaqī differs only in single Khudhū ʿan-nī; differences from Qutayba indicate independent transmission of one Hushaym matn.

partial_common_links.name: Yaʿqūb b. Ibrāhīm al-Dawraqī
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn al-Jārūd and Ibn Ḥibbān agree, but his matn mixes in Shuʿba's verbal clause; he died ~70 years after Hushaym (would have been ~17 at Hushaym's death); scant biography and no written source: accepting him would need an excess of credulity.

partial_common_links.name: ʿAmr b. ʿAwn
partial_common_links.evidence: Occurs only in two collective isnāds (al-Dārimī, al-Bayhaqī) carrying different matns.

partial_common_links.name: Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān
partial_common_links.status: PCL or CL of the Ibn Abī ʿArūba line (p. 183); treated as CL of his own variant (p. 187); one of three (P)CLs of the non-revelation cluster (pp. 188, 218)
partial_common_links.evidence: Abū Dāwūd, al-Maḥāmilī, al-Shāshī and al-Nasāʾī share ramyun/rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra; Ibn Māja's irregular version excluded.

partial_common_links.name: Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj, Hushaym b. Bashīr, Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān
partial_common_links.evidence: Shuʿba and al-Qaṭṭān converge on Qatāda; Hushaym's line reaches al-Ḥasan via Manṣūr b. Zādhān.

partial_common_links.name: Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba and Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj
partial_common_links.status: tentatively conceded as two PCLs of Qatāda
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn Abī ʿArūba's revelation lines share penal-maxim features with Shuʿba and al-Qaṭṭān; since neither Shuʿba nor al-Qaṭṭān has the preamble, Ibn Abī ʿArūba probably transmitted the maxim alone.

partial_common_links.name: Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba, Shuʿba, Yazīd b. Zurayʿ, Hushaym b. Bashīr, Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān
partial_common_links.status: PCLs within a hypothetical scenario only
partial_common_links.evidence: Listed as the PCLs to whom Qatāda's altered tradition would have passed.

partial_common_links.name: Yazīd b. Zurayʿ
partial_common_links.evidence: Cited by al-Nasāʾī and al-Ṭabarī with differing matns; spider above him; if accepted, al-Qaṭṭān would likewise count and Ibn Abī ʿArūba would become an earlier CL; the revelation preamble is likely intrusive in Yazīd's matn.

partial_common_links.status: possible CL/PCL; only with great reservations [S]CL/[S]PCL
partial_common_links.evidence: Abū ʿAwāna and al-Shāshī share al-Ṣaghānī, but double attributions signal doubt; matn draws on both clusters; single strand below.

partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Fākihī (direct CR) are highly consistent; his dictum follows Hushaym's wording.

partial_common_links.name: Ḥammād b. Salama
partial_common_links.evidence: Ibn Ḥanbal and al-ʿAlāʾ agree on the preamble but not the dictum; al-Dārimī's non-revelation variant via Ḥammād lacks the preamble; only a penal-maxim-only version is feasible.

partial_common_links.name: Muʿādh b. Hishām
partial_common_links.evidence: Al-Ṭabarī and Abū ʿAwāna yield a reconstructable preamble and a dictum with Shuʿba's unqualified verbal forms.

partial_common_links.name: Yazīd b. Hārūn
partial_common_links.evidence: Abū ʿUbayd (direct CR) and al-Shāshī no. 1325 differ insignificantly.

partial_common_links.name: Jarīr b. Ḥāzim
partial_common_links.evidence: Al-Ṭayālisī and ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad (via Shaybān) share a preamble citing Q 4:15.

partial_common_links.name: Yūnus b. ʿUbayd
partial_common_links.evidence: Al-Shāfiʿī (with an anonymous trustworthy authority) and al-Nasāʾī differ in several features; matn too unstable to reconstruct.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Ṭabarānī (al-Muʿjam al-Awsaṭ 2:32, no. 1140) ← Aḥmad [b. Isḥāq al-Khashshāb?] ← Abū Jaʿfar al-Nufaylī ← Hushaym
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Matn identical to al-Dawraqī's although al-Dawraqī is absent: an attempted dive under the seeming PCL.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Naḥḥās ← ʿAlī b. Saʿīd b. Bashīr ← ʿAmr b. Rāfiʿ ← Hushaym
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Matches Yaḥyā b. Yaḥyā except single Khudhū ʿan-nī; could be authentic, or Yaḥyā's matn refitted with a new isnād; ʿAlī b. Saʿīd practised tadlīs and transmitted unsupported reports, so he may have devised the isnād.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Muslim ← ʿAmr al-Nāqid ← Hushaym (collective)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Not direct proof of Hushaym's CL status, but indirect support for Yaḥyā b. Yaḥyā as PCL.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Saʿīd b. Manṣūr ← Hushaym (direct CR)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Taghrību ʿāmin probably slipped in from another variant he knew; still a CR corroborating Hushaym.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Dawraqī ← Hushaym (Ibn al-Jārūd, Ibn Ḥibbān)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Pupil would have been about 17 at the teacher's death; matn coined under Shuʿba's influence; not a PCL.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: ʿAlī b. al-Jaʿd ← Shuʿba
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Possible 'age trick' shortening; a written intermediate source could ease the problem, but nothing indicates one for this tradition.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Ṭabarī ← Ibn al-Muthannā ← Ghundar ← Shuʿba
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Three readings: faithful transmission; confusion about provenance with Ibn al-Muthannā chosen as a familiar informant; or proliferation to avoid naming Ibn Ḥanbal, whom al-Ṭabarī never met and whose followers were hostile to him.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Bazzār ← Ibn al-Muthannā ← Ghundar; Muslim's collective isnād via Ibn al-Muthannā/Ibn Bashshār
dives_and_single_strands.type: mismatched matn on a single strand
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Al-Bazzār attached a Hushaym-cluster matn to a Ghundar isnād; Muslim attached a revelation-preamble matn to a non-revelation collective isnād: both judged confused.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Abū ʿAwāna's collective isnād in the Shuʿba cluster (Abū Qilāba / Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Ṣamad / Ibn Junayd)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Matn identical to al-Bazzār's and from the Hushaym cluster; negative value for the Shuʿba analysis; collective isnāds of little utility.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Ṭabarī ← Ibn Bashshār ← ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ← Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba (non-revelation)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: A copy of Shuʿba's tradition with a nominal closing clause; awkward compound; cannot prove Ibn Abī ʿArūba's CL status.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Qaṭṭān ← Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Al-Qaṭṭān, though Shuʿba's companion for twenty years, does not cite Shuʿba; he most likely took Hushaym's version as his base and fitted it with a new isnād through Ibn Abī ʿArūba, a link early biographers do not attest.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Ibn Māja ← Bakr b. Khalaf ← al-Qaṭṭān
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Taghrīb variant of unknown origin lacking al-Qaṭṭān's hallmark; cannot prove his status.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Wakīʿ ← al-Faḍl b. Dalham ← al-Ḥasan ← Qabīsa b. Ḥurayth ← Salama b. al-Muḥabbiq
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Wakīʿ preserved Hushaym's wording but chose an isnād circumventing Ḥiṭṭān and ʿUbāda; rijāl critics suspected forgery.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Ṭabarānī (Awsaṭ 2:286, no. 2002) ← Aḥmad b. Ibrāhīm b. ʿAnbar ← Mūsā b. Maymūn ← Maymūn al-Maraʾī ← al-Ḥasan
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Matn concurs verbatim with Hushaym's; does not establish al-Ḥasan as CL; its maxim differs from Yazīd b. Hārūn's, so at least one tradition was ascribed to Maymūn falsely.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Ibn Abī Ḥātim ← Yūnus b. Ḥabīb ← al-Ṭayālisī ← Mubārak b. Faḍāla ← al-Ḥasan
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Uses rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra, so al-Qaṭṭān may be the original source.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Shāfiʿī ← ʿAbd al-Wahhāb / 'al-thiqa min ahl al-ʿilm' ← Yūnus b. ʿUbayd
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: The anonymous authority damages the isnād and may be a token of manipulation; effectively another single strand.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Isnāds in the Qatāda sub-cluster circumventing Ibn Abī ʿArūba (Ḥammād b. Salama, Muʿādh b. Hishām, Maʿmar, Saʿīd b. Bashīr)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Pavlovitch asks whether they reveal an earlier CL or are mere dives; he reconstructs a Qatāda-level preamble core but cannot establish Qatāda's version of the dictum.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Ibn Ḥanbal / Ibn al-Mundhir / al-Fākihī ← Ḥammād b. Salama ← Qatāda wa-Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl ← al-Ḥasan
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Juxtaposing Ḥumayd and Qatāda on one tier is irregular given their age difference.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: ʿAbd al-Razzāq ← Maʿmar ← Qatāda ← al-Ḥasan (terminates at al-Ḥasan)
dives_and_single_strands.type: defective single strand preserving an early stage
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Read as an early tradition couched as al-Ḥasan's personal opinion; ūḥiya ilā l-nabī is a likely residue of al-Ḥasan's exegetical tradition. Maʿmar and Muʿādh share a source identifiable as Qatāda.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: al-Ṭabarānī (Musnad al-Shāmiyyīn 4:40, no. 2675) ← Aḥmad b. Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā ← Abū al-Jamāhir ← Saʿīd b. Bashīr ← Qatāda
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Mix of early and later matn features on a single line; not unambiguous evidence of Qatāda's CL status.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Yazīd b. Hārūn ← Maymūn b. Mūsā al-Maraʾī ← al-Ḥasan
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Maymūn practised tadlīs from al-Ḥasan, which speaks against the line below Yazīd.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: ʿAbd al-Razzāq ← ʿAbd Allāh b. Muḥarrar ← Ḥiṭṭān ← ʿUbāda
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Ibn Muḥarrar would have to be a nonagenarian or centenarian to have heard Ḥiṭṭān; the matn wording most likely belongs to ʿAbd al-Razzāq himself.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Ibn Ḥanbal 22734, Muslim, Ibn Ḥibbān 4443, al-Shāshī 1320 ← single strands to Ibn Abī ʿArūba
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Maxims agree with the al-Ḥārith and al-Ṣaghānī lines (al-Shāshī 1320 with al-Ṭabarī via Ibn Zurayʿ); perilous to rely on single strands, so Ibn Abī ʿArūba's CL status is not proven.

dives_and_single_strands.strand: Ibn Manda → Abū Nuʿaym → al-Bayhaqī (copying)
dives_and_single_strands.interpretation: Ibn Manda most likely introduced the biographical note on ʿUbāda; Abū Nuʿaym copied it verbatim without naming his source; al-Bayhaqī copied one of them.

clause_scheme.text: Base clause numbering from the Shuʿba matn (Ibn al-Jaʿd, feminine verbs restored): (1) Khudhū ʿan-nī! (2) Qad jaʿala l-lāhu la-hunna sabīlan. (3a) Al-bikru bi-l-bikri (3b) wa-l-thayyibu bi-l-thayyib. (4a) Al-bikru tujlad wa-tunfā (4b) wa-l-thayyibu tujlad wa-turjam.

unqualified verbal forms yujlad/yunfā/yurjam (feminine in Ibn al-Jaʿd)
no number of lashes or period of banishment

genitive compounds jaldu miʾatin, nafyu sana
qualifiers: one hundred lashes, one year
thumma l-rajm / wa-l-rajm as single word

double Khudhū ʿan-nī
Hushaym's qualified compounds
families.reconstructed_wording_as_tabulated: (1) Khudhū ʿan-nī! Khudhū ʿan-nī! (2) Qad jaʿala l-lāhu la-hunna sabīlan. (3a) Al-thayyibu bi-l-thayyibi jaldu miʾatin wa-ramyun bi-l-ḥijāra (3b) wa-l-bikru bi-l-bikri jaldu miʾatin wa-nafyu sana.
families.isnad_correlation: Correlates with the al-Qaṭṭān branch; ramyun/rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra is a version-specific marker used to trace borrowing (al-Ṭabarī via Ibn Zurayʿ, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Abī ʿArūba revelation lines, Muqātil).

distinguishing_elements: Hushaym's wording preserved
isnād detour to Qabīsa b. Ḥurayth and Salama b. al-Muḥabbiq
families.isnad_correlation: Matn does not match its distinct isnād; matn points to Hushaym.

distinguishing_elements: al-Shāfiʿī: taghrību ʿāmin, double exclamation, inverted final clauses
al-Nasāʾī: nafy, single exclamation
families.isnad_correlation: Too unstable to reconstruct a base version.

distinguishing_elements: taghrīb for nafy
families.isnad_correlation: Scattered over several clusters (Abū ʿAwāna, al-Bazzār, Saʿīd b. Manṣūr, al-Shāfiʿī, Ibn Māja); not associated with any CL or PCL.

distinguishing_elements: narratively consistent preamble: Prophet's pallid face and grief (kuriba) at revelation
two-part maxim like Shuʿba
genitive compounds and rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra like al-Qaṭṭān
families.isnad_correlation: Consistent matn traits despite weak isnād evidence; penal maxim wholly dependent on the non-revelation cluster; preamble assembled from generic theophany imagery.

distinguishing_elements: less fictionalized preamble reducible to anna l-nabiyya unzila ʿalay-hi [l-waḥyu] / ūḥiya ilā l-nabī
preamble grammatically disconnected from the dictum
no trace of rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra; dictum alternates between Shuʿba and Hushaym wording
families.isnad_correlation: Preamble core attributable to Qatāda with higher confidence; dictum not uniform across lines.

distinguishing_elements: preamble with grief and pallid face, truncated clause 1b
Ibn Ḥanbal: triple Khudhū ʿan-nī, Shuʿba structure with Hushaym compounds
al-ʿAlāʾ: Hushaym wording
families.isnad_correlation: Preamble shared by Ibn Ḥanbal and al-ʿAlāʾ; dictum diverges by branch.

distinguishing_elements: head-bending preamble without symptoms (al-Ṭabarī), simpler unzila ʿalay-hi dhāta yawmin (Abū ʿAwāna)
dictum with Shuʿba's unqualified verbs (ammā l-thayyibu fa-yujladu thumma yurjam)

(5) Al-thayyibu bi-l-thayyibi wa-l-bikru bi-l-bikr (6a) Ammā l-thayyibu fa-yujladu thumma yurjam (6b) wa-ammā l-bikru fa-yujladu thumma yunfā
families.isnad_correlation: Both branches above Muʿādh share the dictum, which tracks Shuʿba.

distinguishing_elements: ūḥiya ilā l-nabī with no symptoms
Khudhū! Khudhū! without min-nī
Hushaym-type maxim
families.isnad_correlation: Preamble shares a source with Muʿādh's (Qatāda); maxim does not.

interjected qāla [?]

Hushaym-type maxim

Iqbalū-hunna! (3) Qad jaʿala l-lāhu la-hunna sabīlan. (4a) Al-bikru bi-l-bikri jaldu miʾatin thumma nafyu ʿāmin (4b) wa-l-thayyibu bi-l-thayyibi jaldu miʾatin thumma l-rajm.
families.isnad_correlation: Preamble later than Muʿādh's and Qatāda's reconstructed versions; the feminine-plural exclamation is read as a relic of al-Ḥasan's tradition.

families.family: Jarīr b. Ḥāzim / al-Ḥasan's exegetical core
distinguishing_elements: explicit citation of Q 4:15 (al-Ṭayālisī: aw yajʿala l-lāhu la-hunna sabīlan; ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad: wa-l-lātī yaʾtīna l-fāḥishata)
passive verbs (unzilat, rufiʿa)
al-Ṭayālisī: Khudhū ḥidhra-kum! (Hyderabad ed.) vs Khudhū! Khudhū! (al-Turkī ed.)
families.reconstructed_wording_as_tabulated: Jarīr: Unzilat 'Qurʾān 4:15' fa-lammā rufiʿa l-waḥyu qāla rasūlu l-lāhi, ṣalʿam. Al-Ḥasan: (1) Unzilat 'Qurʾān 4:15' fa-lammā rufiʿa l-waḥyu qāla rasūlu l-lāhi, ṣalʿam: (2) 'Khudhū-hunna! Iqbalū-hunna!'
families.isnad_correlation: Two independent lines via Jarīr agree on the Q 4:15 core; the exclamation is supplied from Yazīd b. Hārūn's line.

distinguishing_elements: opens Allāhu akbar! Jāʾa l-lāhu bi-l-sabīl (paraphrase of Q 4:15) instead of Khudhū ʿan-nī
clause 3 reproduces al-Qaṭṭān verbatim (rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra)
no revelation preamble
families.isnad_correlation: Not applicable; used to test the literary dating.

development_sequence.step: Shuʿba's unqualified two-part maxim with verbal forms
Hushaym merges clauses, adds genitive compounds and quantity/duration qualifiers
al-Qaṭṭān substitutes ramyun bi-l-ḥijāra for rajm for syntactic uniformity; later transmitters partly restore rajm as rajmun bi-l-ḥijāra; Wakīʿ restores Hushaym's wording
Revelation preamble (from al-Ḥasan's Q 4:15 tradition) attached to non-revelation dictums and progressively fictionalized (pallid face, grief, closed eyes, silence)

revelation_preamble_layers.text: The preamble divides into a symptoms layer (tarabbada wajhu-hu, kuriba li-dhālika) and a structural layer (kāna ... idhā nazala/nuzzila ʿalay-hi; fa-nazala ... dhāta yawmin fa-lammā surriya ʿan-hu qāla). Its fictional units are generic theophany descriptions, not unique to this tradition.

non_revelation.finding: Strong: matn development lines up with the CL sequence Shuʿba → Hushaym → al-Qaṭṭān, and version-specific features identify borrowings where matn and isnād disagree (al-Bazzār, Abū ʿAwāna, al-Dawraqī, al-Dārimī, Wakīʿ, al-Ṭabarī via Ibn Abī ʿArūba).

revelation.finding: Weak: penal parts are compounds of the three non-revelation versions attached erratically to the preamble; revelation symptoms are distributed haphazardly and cannot be tied to specific CLs.

criteria_used.criterion: Qualified (specific) wording is later than vague wording
Lectio difficilior signals the earlier version
Removal of fictionalization layers to reach a narrative core
Passive verbal forms treated as older units of expression
Clause order is fluid and its reversal is not evidence of a different source

dating_conclusion.summary: The non-revelation dual-penalty tradition goes back to Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj and existed by the second quarter of the second century AH (before ca. 150 AH); Hushaym, al-Qaṭṭān and Wakīʿ produced variants in the second half of that century. The revelation preamble derives from a short exegetical tradition of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. 110/728) applying Q 4:15, which is the earliest reconstructable form in the bundle; it contained no dual-penalty maxim. The compound revelation tradition took shape from the last quarter of the second century to the start of the third century AH.

items.claim: Hushaym's variant shows the non-revelation tradition existed around the middle of the second century AH; Shuʿba's unqualified form must be earlier, so the tradition existed as early as the second quarter of the second century AH.

Variants circulated in Iraqi centres during the second half of the second century AH, based on the version Shuʿba spread before the middle of that century; al-Qaṭṭān and Wakīʿ spread variants during its last quarter.
The base legal requirements had their final shape in the second quarter of the second century AH; none of the non-revelation variants presents the dictum as revealed.
Earliest attestable variant of the non-revelation tradition: Shuʿba's reconstructed matn (table).

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. 110/728) most likely circulated a short exegetical tradition: Q 4:15 was revealed and, when revelation withdrew, the Prophet said 'Take them! Accept them!'; it refers to no extra-Quranic source of law.

The revelation tradition developed during the last decades of the second century AH and the beginning of the third, from originally independent narratives (the three non-revelation variants and al-Ḥasan's preamble).

Collection evidence indicates the preamble was attached to the maxim only towards the end of the second century AH, long after Qatāda and Ibn Abī ʿArūba died; al-Ṭayālisī's Musnad holds the earliest surviving compound, ʿAbd al-Razzāq's a more edited one, and Abū ʿUbayd's the completed form.
By the beginning of the second quarter of the third century AH the revelation narrative had acquired its final shape.
The merger of the two originally independent traditions started some time in the last quarter of the second century AH.

Literary analysis alone: no sunnaic material in the exegesis for most of the second century; a prophetic dual-penalty tradition circulated towards its end; shortly after, it was perceived as divinely inspired while some exegetes posited a stoning verse; the Māʿiz and servant traditions entered the debate probably in the last quarter of the third century AH.

Muqātil's dictum reproduces al-Qaṭṭān's wording and so postdates Muqātil by at least 25 years: it is a later addition, matching the literary analysis; its paraphrastic opening clauses may preserve an earlier stage, and the Khudhū ʿan-nī/Q 4:15 clauses took final shape only in the third century AH.
Contrary to Juynboll, the dual-penalty maxim was not a factor in the legal debates of al-Ḥasan's floruit, still less in early Islam.

If al-Ḥasan relied on the scriptural ruling, scripture (or what became the textus receptus) was a basis for legal derivation by the end of the first century AH; in zinā, scripture is the primary stage and the sunnaic ʿUbāda ruling a second-century secondary stage. Preliminary, pending study of other zinā traditions.

earliest_reconstructable_form.dual_penalty_maxim_earliest: Shuʿba b. al-Ḥajjāj's matn (d. 160/776), dated to the second quarter of the second century AH

methodological_positions.topic: Key figure vs CL vs PCL vs SCL
methodological_positions.position: States in definite terms a distinction Juynboll only alluded to: a key figure is any branching point; the CL is the earliest key figure provably circulating the tradition; an oldest key figure may prove a seeming CL.

relation.stance: departs (Görke uses key figure and CL synonymously)

methodological_positions.position: Reviews Juynboll (CL invented the single strand to the Prophet), Motzki (CL as first systematic collector, tradition older than CL) and Calder (CL produced by later mutual isnād criticism) without formally adopting one.
A key figure from which only single strands branch is a seeming CL, following Juynboll's skeptical approach; concurring spider matns are suspect of isnād proliferation.
One tenable PCL plus single strands proves a CL only with qualifications; two tenable PCLs plus concurring single strands suffice; three or more PCLs make the case obvious.

methodological_positions.topic: Direct collector citations of a key figure
methodological_positions.position: An unmediated single-strand quotation by a CR has every chance of representing a real teacher-pupil link unless proven otherwise and should not be dismissed automatically as part of a spider; more CRs strengthen a key figure's CL/PCL status.

relation.stance: draws on a similar criterion (a tradition is at least as old as the collection containing it)

methodological_positions.topic: Alignment with Motzki on single strands and collector perspective
methodological_positions.position: His CR rule and his willingness to use single strands under extra criteria resemble Motzki's view (cited in n. 4) that single strands can be authentic and isnāds should be read from the collector's side; Pavlovitch does not state this alignment himself.
Endorses Motzki's criticism of Juynboll for drawing conclusions from silence (absence of a tradition from a collection).

methodological_positions.topic: Own use of silence in literary analysis
methodological_positions.position: In the literary section he nonetheless defines a terminus post quem for the dual-penalty dispute 'by an argument from silence' (Ibn Ḥanbal, Ibn Qutayba).

Late synoptic rijāl works seem to recover names retrospectively from isnāds; relying on them for obscure tradents is circular, so he prefers contemporary or near-contemporary rijāl works. He cites Berg's 'symbiotic' view and Motzki's rebuttal, and adds Melchert's report on al-Bukhārī as a point Motzki may have overlooked.

relation.stance: notes Juynboll's later caution about single-strand fulāns

methodological_positions.position: Treats implausibly long teacher-pupil spans as possible isnād-shortening devices, citing Juynboll; applied to Ibn al-Jaʿd and al-Dawraqī, and to ʿAbd Allāh b. Muḥarrar.
Collective isnāds cannot show which transmitter originated a matn's wording; of little utility and highly unreliable for dating.

methodological_positions.topic: Matn consistency for short legal traditions
methodological_positions.position: Motif overlap that works for long historical narratives is not enough for terse legal pronouncements; only matns with limited structural instability attributable to transmission belong to a CL/PCL; deeper reconstructions are more tentative.

relation.stance: qualifies their narrative-motif approach for legal traditions
acknowledges critique that reconstructed cores are tiny

methodological_positions.position: Fictional layers (place, time, actors, emotions) can be peeled off to reach a core; fictionalization does not preclude authenticity.
Single strands are perilous evidence except where CR citation, overlap with established CL variants, or narrative peculiarities (vaguer formulations, difficult readings) allow assessment.
Juynboll's al-Ḥasan conclusion contradicts his own isnād criteria and rests on Schacht's maxim principle; isnād-only analysis leaves the wording of 'basic elements' to intuition.

Uses Wansbrough's exegetical typology and degree of conceptual refinement (after Schacht, Coulson, Melchert) for relative dating, then tests it against isnād-cum-matn results; concludes the methods are complementary, can coincide, and literary analysis is indispensable when isnād evidence is absent or indecisive.
Rejects Wansbrough's claim that Qurʾān vs sunna status was hardly operative in Abū ʿUbayd's rules.
When isnād evidence is contradictory, the earliest surviving collections (al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Abū ʿUbayd) are used to trace the compound tradition's growth.

Proposes an 'organic development' with repeated editorial deletions and accretions and third-century back-projection onto Qatāda and Ibn Abī ʿArūba to accommodate inconsistencies that cannot be fully resolved.

Against Schacht's view that law based on the Qurʾān beyond the perfunctory is secondary, the zinā case shows scripture as the primary stage and sunna as secondary; chronologically overlaps Crone's mid-Umayyad date for canonical scripture while differing from the Burton/Crone emphasis on a Qurʾān-sunna rupture. Preliminary.

If Ibn Ḥanbal discussed the dual penalty, the date 'will have to be pushed back to the first half of the second century AH'; given Ibn Ḥanbal's death in 241, the third century seems meant.
